opus-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to put it is that language is a very late invention, both evolutionarily and developmentally. Animals have world models. A cat jumping onto a table has to predict how its body will move, where the edge is, whether the surface will hold. There's no language involved at all. A baby understands object permanence and gravity, and that things don't pass through each other, long before they can say a single word. So the world model in our brain is grounded first in perception and action, in vision, touch, and moving around. Language sits on top of that.

A language model learns from text, and text is something humans have already heavily compressed and abstracted. When I write "the cup fell off the table," that sentence assumes you already know what a cup is, what falling looks like, what happens when it hits the floor. The language model only sees the symbols. It can learn a lot of the statistical structure of how we talk about the world, which is impressive and very useful. But it's like learning about the world from someone else's diary rather than living in it.

Another difference is what you're predicting. A language model predicts the next token, a discrete thing from a finite vocabulary. A world model is predicting how the state of the world evolves, often conditioned on an action: if I do this, what happens next? That state is continuous, high-dimensional, noisy, and mostly irrelevant detail. You don't predict every pixel or every leaf moving in the wind. You need some abstract representation that keeps what matters for planning and drops the rest. That's a much harder problem than next-token prediction. I'd argue it's also the more fundamental one.

So my view is that language models are a kind of shortcut. They borrow the intelligence humans have already distilled into text, which is why they got so good so fast. But if we want systems that truly understand physical space, can plan, and can act in the real world, we can't skip the part where the model learns from sensory experience. Vision in particular is a huge piece of that. That's a big reason I've been pushing on visual representation learning and spatial intelligence rather than treating vision as just an input adapter bolted onto an LLM.

They aren't opposites. Eventually you want both: a grounded world model, and language as an interface for reasoning and communication on top of it. I just think the field has been a little upside down, building the roof first and hoping the foundation emerges on its own.

r002.rationale: It describes language as an interface for reasoning and communication, but does not distinguish language-model use as purpose-driven communication.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that a language model is a model of what people say, and a world model is a model of what actually happens.

If you think about how a child learns, they don't start with language. They start by watching things fall, by reaching for objects, by seeing that when they push a cup it moves and when they let go it drops. All of that gets built up long before they have any words for "gravity" or "cup." That's the world model. It's a model of physical and spatial reality, of cause and effect, of how things unfold over time. And it's fundamentally grounded in perception and action. It lives in a continuous, high-dimensional space, not in discrete tokens.

Language comes later, and it's a kind of compression. Humans took this incredibly rich understanding of the world and found a way to encode a tiny slice of it into symbols so we could communicate it to each other. So when a language model learns from text, it's learning from the shadow of the world model, not the world model itself. It gets a lot, because humans wrote down a lot. But it never gets the part that was too obvious to write down. Nobody writes "when I turned the corner the building was still there." Nobody writes down what it feels like to catch a ball. That stuff is implicit, and it's exactly what the brain's world model is made of.

So the way I'd distinguish them is this. The language model is extremely good at the parts of the world that have been verbalized. The brain's world model is good at everything, including the enormous majority of experience that never gets verbalized at all. And I think that's why if you want to build something that really understands space, physics, and how to act in the world, you can't just scale text. You have to go back to the sensory stream, to video, to embodiment, and learn the model the way the brain learned it, from the bottom up.

r002.rationale: It says language helps people communicate and that language models learn from text, but does not distinguish language-model use as purpose-driven communication.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is that our understanding of the world is grounded in perception and action. We see things, touch them, move around, and observe what happens when we do something. Language is one way we express that understanding, but it isn’t the whole thing. You can predict that a cup will fall if you push it off a table without describing that prediction in words.

A language model learns primarily from how things are represented in language. And language contains an enormous amount of knowledge about the world, so predicting text can lead a model to learn meaningful structure. I wouldn’t say a language model necessarily has no world model. The question is what kind of world model it learns, and where that model breaks down.

For me, the interesting test is whether a system can use its understanding to predict the consequences of actions in new situations. Can it update its beliefs from what it observes? Can it distinguish a plausible description from something that would actually happen? Those are stronger tests than whether it can give a convincing verbal explanation.

So I see language as an important part of the picture, but perception, action, and feedback are central to the kind of world understanding we have.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is that our brain’s model of the world is grounded in perception and action. We see things, interact with them, and learn what happens as a consequence. If I push a cup toward the edge of a table, I can anticipate that it might fall. I don’t need to describe that situation in language to make the prediction.

A language model learns primarily through language, which contains an enormous amount of information about the world. So I wouldn’t say it has no world model. Predicting language well may require learning some underlying structure of the world. But learning from descriptions of experiences is different from learning through those experiences.

For me, the interesting question is how to connect those things: language, perception, action, and the ability to predict consequences. And we should test that ability in new situations, rather than assume that a convincing verbal explanation means the model understands how the world works.
